bound.my_view: The framing is correct and honest. Only an unparseable file pays anything (fast path returns at line 250 with pauses=0), so the healthy 170+ corpus and the 9 known gap files cost exactly nothing -- measured: readable 0.0002 s, live audit retried []. Correctness of branch (d) does not depend on the window at all: a file that never moves is a settled defect at 0.8 s exactly as at 0 ms, and exhaustion-while-moving is already a skip. Two residual risks I would NOT call regressions: (i) a genuinely torn write frozen longer than 0.8 s on a loaded machine is still a hard failure -- that is disclosed, and only a writer-side temp+rename removes it; (ii) the cost is per-suspect-file, so an anomalous run with N unparseable files pays N*0.8 s wall clock, a latency cost never a false failure. The one place the wording could mislead: 'a slow writer is skipped, never failed' is true only for a writer that MOVES during the watch; one that pauses past it is failed, as the docstring itself says.

residuals.docstring_quote: THE OVERSTATEMENT THIS CORRECTS (U8.35).  The old claim -- "a torn read is not [stable], so the guard does not flicker" -- was too strong, for exactly V8.29's reason: a torn file whose writer pauses for longer than the window presents the same bytes to every read, looks settled, and is still reported as a defect.  The loop does NOT remove that exposure and this docstring no longer says it does; no finite window can outlast a writer that pauses longer than the window. ... SETTLE_DELAY_S and SETTLE_MAX_ATTEMPTS are therefore a LATENCY budget, not a correctness one.  ||  Recorded residual exposure (deliberate, not hidden): a tear that leaves a VALID but incomplete JSON object (so it parses and is accepted on the first read) is not caught by this loop.  It is not caught by the old one either, closing it would make every known baseline-gap file pay the pause on every run, and a truncation of a JSON document essentially never yields a parseable object.
residuals.what_actually_happens: A tear yielding valid JSON is judged SETTLED on the first read (pauses=0, retried [], cost 0.0001 s) and is never a parse failure. Its fate then depends on the keys it kept: (i) if all seven unit-contract keys survive (my C4a: all keys present, a field emptied/truncated) it is accepted into docs with failures [] and gaps {} -- the guard and the whole suite pass it silently, which is strictly more than the docstring's 'not caught by this loop' wording; (ii) if the tear cut keys off (my C4b) it is still accepted on the first read but surfaces as a key GAP, so test_no_new_contract_key_gaps only catches it for a name not already frozen in a baseline -- for a baseline-known name it is absorbed. This is the sharpest residual and it is real, but it is DISCLOSED, and a genuine prefix tear of an indent=2 handoff is next to unable to yield balanced JSON (every prefix ends mid-nesting), so case (i) needs a contrived complete-but-stubbed document rather than a natural torn write.

tightenings.would_break_on: A CPython release whose json message for the frozen U0.22 bytes stops containing the lowercase word 'delimiter' (the position literal is no longer load-bearing, so renumbering does NOT break it). It would then fail LOUDLY on the fixture, not silently pass: the new form is a conjunction requiring both the exception-class prefix (produced by _parse itself as '%s: %s' % (type(exc).__name__, exc), so stable) and the wording. The old disjunction could pass with the position evidence entirely absent, and would have kept passing after a renumber -- so this is strictly tighter at the cost of depending on one English word in a frozen input's message.
